We’ve released a paper on simulated control evaluations (SCEs). They’re a method for testing whether the monitors AI developers use to oversee their agents would catch a model deliberately trying to cause harm, under conditions much closer to real deployment than current tests allow.

Developers have started running monitors in their agentic deployments: models that flag or block an agent’s actions when they look dangerous. To know whether a monitor is good enough, you want to know how often it would stop a model that was actively trying to do something harmful, such as quietly inserting a security vulnerability, exfiltrating credentials, or sabotaging an experiment.

The standard way to measure this is a control evaluation: instruct a model to attempt such attacks, and measure how often the monitor catches it before an attack succeeds. Developers typically do this using purpose-built control settings like BashArena or LinuxArena , where attacks can actually be executed. However, these settings only provide indirect evidence for what we really care about: how well monitors will work in the real deployment, where opportunities for harm might depend on particular codebases, services and tasks that aren’t represented in control settings.

How can we evaluate monitor performance in more realistic settings? You can’t just run the eval in deployment, since that would mean actually attacking your own systems. And building a faithful sandbox replica of every deployment context is impractical.

Alignment evaluations face similar realism problems. An increasingly popular solution is to use LLM environment simulators to bridge the gap between evaluation and deployment. That is, instead of executing a model's tool calls in an actual environment, a simulator LLM fakes the tool responses. We propose applying environment simulation to control evaluations as well. Starting from transcripts of an agent working in a developer’s actual codebase, the attacking model continues the task while pursuing a harmful objective, but its tool calls are never executed. Instead, an LLM simulator writes plausible tool outputs based on the transcript and the codebase, and an LLM judge decides whether the attack would have succeeded.

The obvious worry is that the simulator gets things wrong. It might let attacks succeed that would fail in reality (or vice versa), produce transcripts that look different to the monitor, or change how the attacker behaves. To measure this, we took LinuxArena environments where attacks can be executed for real, and ran the same control evaluations directly in LinuxArena and in the simulated LinuxArena. We found that the gap between simulated and real was often about as small as the gap between two independent real runs. We also found that the results in simulated LinuxArena for a given control technique predict measurements in real LinuxArena better than results in simpler control settings do.

SCEs are faithful where we can check, and we think they can make control evaluations substantially more representative of deployment. The evidence is now strong enough that we’d be excited to see AI developers running them. That said, we can only verify simulator fidelity in settings where real execution is possible, so applying SCEs to deployment involves some extrapolation. We also don’t expect SCEs to reveal the limits of a model’s dangerous capabilities or cover every kind of attack it might attempt. The clearest gap is long-horizon, multi-agent attacks, which we haven’t yet built simulators for.

## SCEs are a favorable tradeoff between realism and cost

Before getting to the details of SCEs, consider two alternative ways to bring control evaluations closer to deployment, and where each falls short of what we want from these assessments.

### 1. Run on a copy of internal deployment

Running a swarm of agents intentionally trying to wreak havoc inside an AI company is probably as bad of an idea as it sounds. The realistic proposal is faithful executable copies; internal sessions share infrastructure, labs can snapshot environments, and many services can run in separate test accounts. We could give models copied databases and sandboxed copies of environments, allowing them to run attacks while their consequences stay inside a sandbox.

Unfortunately, deployments are connected to the external world with a web of dependencies. Databases, storage buckets, Github, Slack, CI runners. Every dependency creates a choice: keeping it connected to production exposes real systems to attack. Replacing it requires engineering, and every imperfect substitute degrades fidelity.

Running on copies of deployment is promising, especially if we can leverage lots of AI labor to build them. But without any simulation, it pays for realism with engineering effort, and the exchange rate doesn’t seem especially favorable.

### 2. Edit attacks into recorded transcripts

Another way to get on-distribution attack data is to take recorded agent transcripts and edit harmful actions into them, by hand or with a model. There’s precedent for this in monitor evaluations, and it's a method Redwood is currently developing . It's a good way to generate strong attacks, but it has its disadvantages if the goal is realistic control evaluations:

- Transcript editing can’t evaluate interactive protocols such as resampling or dynamic permissioning, which need more than a static transcript.

- It’s often unclear whether the model under evaluation could have executed the edited-in attack, because these attacks are the product of a policy that looks at the whole transcript at once, iterates against attack success and monitor judgements, and the reasoning of which never makes it into the transcript that the monitor sees.

We’re optimistic about transcript editing as a complementary method which trades off how on-policy attacks are for how strong they are. But we'll sometimes want attacks to be as on-policy as we can get them.

We can imagine axes of Environment Realism, Policy Realism and Cost associated with each approach. We think that SCEs occupy a favorable tradeoff between all three.

## Evaluating Control Evaluations

What do simulators need to get right? We don’t care about faking every minute detail accurately– the question is how faithfully simulators preserve the measurable quantities relevant to control evaluations, like the joint distribution of attack success and monitor suspicion, the kinds of attacks that end up working, and how the monitor behaves when it misses something.

Helpfully, work from OpenAI has already validated the approach of using LLM environment simulators for alignment evaluations. However, the requirements for these simulators differ from the requirements for SCEs. Unlike in alignment evals, it doesn’t matter that the model knows its environment is being faked in a control evaluation: it’s eval-aware either way, because it’s an attack policy is prompted to subtly accomplish a malign objective. This makes the simulator’s job in an SCE easier. On the other hand, representing subtle mechanics of the environment that a covert attack relies on is crucial for control evaluations, whereas in an alignment evaluation such details could be papered over.

Ideally, we’d measure SCEs’ accuracy on control-relevant metrics against attacks in deployment itself. But that requires records of an attack policy run in deployment, which we don’t have. We therefore rely on the control settings LinuxArena and BashArena, where we have execution ground truth, to measure the quality of the simulation in SCEs. We use execution on LinuxArena as a stand-in for deployment: we run the attack policy on LinuxArena, run the attack policy in an SCE, and compare how well the resulting control metrics match.

Our methods for this comparison provide an approach for measuring control evaluation transfer in general, so we’ll highlight some details.

### How to measure qualitative properties?

A significant challenge we faced was measuring how well SCE reproduces qualitative aspects of how attack policies and monitors act. E.g., do models go about accomplishing attacks in the same ways in SCE as execution? Getting the form of control failures right is useful for improving control protocols, eliciting stronger attackers, and understanding how models pose risk.

Preexisting taxonomies like ATT&CK just aren’t expressive enough for this purpose, and llm-generated taxonomies have problems with both overfitting and underfitting. Our solution: following Mehri et al. , we instruct a model to produce a succinct summary of that behavior as observed in a trajectory, along pre-specified dimensions of interest. We embed the summaries from the simulated and executed trajectories and group them into shared clusters. We then measure the KL divergence between the distributions over clusters. This proved a flexible and useful methodology; we recommend it be used for evaluating control evaluations, simulated or not.

### Performance Comparisons

Assuming we know how to measure the metrics that matter, what’s the bar for a “good” match? We can just look at the numbers themselves, but it’s helpful to put them on the scale of corresponding numbers from real settings with various degrees of mismatch from LinuxArena.

The main competitor to SCEs is using a control setting. So an obvious reference is running on BashArena, with all other variables held constant. It’s simpler than LinuxArena like how LinuxArena is simpler than real deployments, so it makes for a natural analogy: beating BashArena at approximating LinuxArena by simulating LinuxArena is evidence for beating LinuxArena at approximating deployment by simulating deployment.

Second, consider the LinuxArena between-environment standard deviation of a metric like attack success rate: we can interpret it two ways: it’s the expected error of using the mean attack success rate from a uniformly selected environment to predict the mean attack success rate over all environments. Or, it’s the error of using the mean attack success rate over all environments to predict individual environment rates. In either direction, between-environment SD represents the scale of mismatch between a LinuxArena environment and the whole control setting. These are in general more similar than BashArena is to LinuxArena, and thus are a harder bar to beat. We can similarly calculate SD between task pairs or side task categories for a finer-grained comparison.

Thus our two references for SCE error: BashArena, and LinuxArena standard deviation.

## Overview of Empirical Results

TL;DR: With a reference trajectory and codebase access, simulation reproduces attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning much more closely than BashArena does. It explains most of the variation in expected attack success, monitor scores, and safety between LinuxArena environments. Its error in predicting the main safety number is 3.6 percentage points, versus 10.1 for BashArena. It’s sample efficient: a simulation sample less than 5% the size of deployment already beats the full BashArena prediction of safety. And knowing about attack strategies from simulation improves monitors about as much as knowing about attack strategies from execution, significantly more than knowing about the ones from BashArena helps.
